title: type vs interface
subtitle: Object shapes, merging, unions, and when to pick each

cards.front: Plain object shape — interface or type?
cards.meaning: Both can describe object shapes and overlap heavily day to day. For a plain object with no unions or mapped types, either works. Consistency in a codebase often matters more than the pick.
cards.example:
interface UserI { id: string; name: string }
type UserT = { id: string; name: string }

cards.front: Do interface and type survive as runtime values?
cards.meaning: No. Both are structural, both are erased, neither supports instanceof. Runtime validation (zod, class-validator) is a separate concern.

Object shape: both. Declaration merging: interface only (same-name type is a duplicate-identifier error). Unions, tuples/primitives, mapped/conditional: type only. implements: both when the type is object-shaped. Composition: interface extends (multiple allowed); type uses &.

Multiple interface declarations with the same name in the same scope merge into one interface with all members combined. Type aliases with the same name are a duplicate-identifier error — they do not merge.

cards.front: Why prefer interface for Express Request.user?
cards.meaning: Declaration merging. You can augment third-party or global types without forking: Express Request with user after auth middleware (Nest), fields on Window / Node globals, plugin APIs. A second interface Request { user: User } merges; redeclaring a type with the same name is a compile error.

Reopen the library's interface inside declare module so Request gains user. Merging only works when you augment the correct module or global scope — wrong module name is a common miss. Exact module name varies by Express typings version.

extends reads clearly for “object is a specialization of another object,” allows multiple extends, and errors on conflicting incompatible members. & also composes object types and participates in a wider algebra (unions, conditionals). Intersecting contradictory property types can yield never for that property — & is not always “extends with nicer errors.”

cards.front: Can interface name a union of variants?
cards.meaning: No at the top level. A type alias can be A | B; an interface cannot express that union as the alias itself. Object members of an interface can use union field types, but the alias itself cannot be a union.
cards.example: type Result = { ok: true; value: string } | { ok: false; error: string }

cards.meaning: Use type. Interfaces cannot alias primitives, tuples like [string, number], or recursive Json-style unions the way type aliases can.

cards.front: Mapped / conditional types — interface or type?
cards.meaning: Only type aliases. If your shape needs mapping over keys, you are in type land. Utility types are built this way.
cards.example:
type ReadonlyPartial<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };
type NonNullableField<T> = T extends null | undefined ? never : T

cards.front: Can a class implements a type alias?
cards.meaning: Yes, when the alias describes an object shape. implements is a compile-time check that the instance shape matches — it does not invent a runtime interface object. Prefer interface for public OOP-style APIs for the conventional reading, not because type cannot work.
cards.example:
type AlsoPrintable = { print(): void };
class Doc2 implements AlsoPrintable { print() {} }

cards.front: Does type skip excess property checks?
cards.meaning: No. Fresh object literals assigned to a target type get excess property checking whether the target was declared with interface or type. The rule is fresh literals plus target type, not the keyword.
cards.example:
f({ x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }); // Error — excess z (PointI)
g({ x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }); // Error — same (PointT)

cards.meaning: Default to interface for public object shapes — props, DTOs, API responses — because extends reads clearly and merging is occasionally useful (Express Request). Reach for type for unions, tuples, mapped/conditional types, or when intersections compose better than an extends chain. Do not dogmatically always-interface or always-type.

cards.front: DTO extends BaseDto vs A & B where A might be a union?
cards.meaning: For “DTO extends BaseDto,” interface extends is often the clearest. For “A & B & C where A might be a union,” type plus & fits.

cards.front: Are interfaces faster for the checker?
cards.meaning: Interfaces can be slightly cheaper for the checker in huge codebases in some historical/edge cases. Rarely decisive for app code. Do not lead an interview with “interfaces are faster” — lead with expressiveness and merging.
